title: Singly Linked List
tagline: Singly linked list nodes, head and tail, insertion, deletion, reversal, traversal, emptiness checks, and linked-list versus array trade-offs.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original BoardPrep study material for the CISCE ISC Class XII Computer Science syllabus (subject code 868), examination year 2027, Section C. The syllabus topic list was taken from the verified 2027 syllabus; the explanations, examples and questions here are original and were not taken from any board examination paper, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: A singly linked list is one of the simplest dynamic data structures: a chain of nodes, each holding a value and a reference to the next node. This chapter explains how a linked list is built, how to traverse it, and how to insert, delete and reverse nodes by changing references. It also compares linked lists with arrays, so you can see when a linked list is a good choice and when it is not.

learn.title: What a singly linked list is

blocks.text: A singly linked list is a linear data structure made of nodes, where each node holds a value and a reference to the next node. The first node is called the head. The last node usually has a null reference, meaning there is no next node. Unlike an array, the nodes are not stored in consecutive memory, and the list does not have a fixed size in the same way an array does. A linked list grows and shrinks by adding and removing nodes as references are updated.

The main idea is that the list is a chain of nodes. To reach a node, you usually start at the head and follow the references one by one. You cannot jump directly to the fifth node by position the way you can with an array. That makes a linked list good for some things and awkward for others. It is good when you need to add or remove nodes without shifting a whole block of elements, and it is awkward when you need repeated fast access by position.

Each node holds a value and a reference to the next node.
The first node is the head; the last node usually links to null.

blocks.text: Traversal means visiting each node in order. To traverse a singly linked list, you start at the head and follow the next references until you reach null. This is the fundamental way to read the contents of a linked list. If you want to print every value, search for a value, count the nodes, or find the middle of the list, you usually traverse the list from the head.

Traversal is simple in concept but it is central to almost every linked list operation. Insertion, deletion and many kinds of inspection all depend on moving along the links correctly. A common mistake is to forget to advance the reference during traversal, or to stop one node too early. In an examination trace, you are often asked to follow the links step by step and say what the list looks like after each change.

items.note: Start at the head (10), move to the next node (20), move to the next node (30), then reach null and stop.

learn.title: Inserting nodes in a linked list

blocks.text: Insertion is one of the operations a linked list makes relatively easy. You can insert at the head, at the tail, or in the middle. Inserting at the head is the simplest: you create a new node whose next reference points to the current head, then make the head point to the new node. That operation does not require traversing the whole list. Inserting at the tail requires reaching the last node first, unless you already keep a tail reference.

Inserting in the middle is where care is needed. To insert a node between two existing nodes, you must find the node before the insertion point, set the new node’s next reference to the later node, and then update the previous node’s next reference to the new node. If you get the order wrong, you can lose the rest of the list. The exact order of updates matters every time.

learn.title: Deleting nodes from a linked list

blocks.text: Deletion means removing a node from the list. The simplest case is deleting the head. You make the head point to the next node, and the old head is no longer part of the list. Deleting the last node requires finding the node before it and setting its next to null. Deleting a node in the middle requires finding the node before the one to delete, then skipping over the deleted node by linking the previous node directly to the node after it.

A linked list must be handled carefully during deletion because if you lose a reference to a node, you lose the rest of the list after it. That is why deletion usually works from the node before the target node rather than from the target node itself. The exam often checks whether you can trace a deletion and describe what the list looks like afterward.

items.note: Make the head point to the second node; the old first node is removed from the list.

blocks.text: Reversing a linked list means changing the direction of the links so that the last node becomes the first and the first becomes the last. This is a classic linked list operation. The basic idea is to walk along the list and, for each node, make its next reference point to the node you came from instead of the node you are going to. You have to keep track of three references at a time: the current node, the node before it, and the node after it.

Reversal is not just a trick; it shows that a linked list can be reorganized by changing references without moving data. It is also a good examination topic because it requires careful use of temporary references. If you reverse a short list by hand, you can trace exactly how the head changes and how each node’s next reference is redirected.

items.note: After reversal, the head becomes the node that held 30, and the links become 30 -> 20 -> 10 -> null.

learn.title: Empty lists, length and boundary cases

blocks.text: An empty linked list has no nodes. Its head is usually null, and most operations must check for that case before doing anything else. Trying to remove from an empty list, or searching an empty list, should be handled as a boundary case rather than assumed never to happen. Many linked list bugs come from forgetting the empty case or forgetting the single-node case.

Length is another basic property. The length of a linked list is the number of nodes it contains. To find the length, you usually traverse the entire list and count the nodes, unless you maintain a separate length variable. The single-node list is a special case worth remembering: removing the only node should leave an empty list, and inserting into an empty list should make that node the head.

items: An empty list has a null head.

blocks.text: A linked list and an array both store sequences of values, but they do it differently. An array stores values in consecutive memory and allows fast access by position. A linked list stores nodes with links and does not require consecutive memory. The advantage of a linked list is that you can insert and delete without moving other elements. The disadvantage is that you cannot access a node by position quickly; you have to follow the links.

This trade-off is a recurring theme in computer science. If your program needs frequent insertions and deletions, especially away from the ends, a linked list may be a reasonable choice. If your program needs fast access by index, an array is usually better. The syllabus expects you to understand this difference, not just to memorize the definition of a linked list.

Linked lists allow insertion and deletion without shifting.
Linked lists do not support fast random access.
The best choice depends on the operations a program needs.

Accessing elements in order by following links or positions one at a time.
